newsitem.title: USA: Consumer group urges caution on power deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Consumer group urges caution on power deregulation.

text.p: A consumer policy group Wednesday said the U.S. government should let states set the pace for deregulating power markets, otherwise small consumers might be hurt in a rush to break up utility monopolies.

Joining the debate on whether Congress should force states to open local power markets, the Competition Policy Institute urged lawmakers not to set a deadline, but make it easy for states to promote competition.
"Consumers can benefit from additional competition in the electric industy, but only if it is done right," said Ron Binz, lead author of a report by the institute.
The institute is funded by telecommunications firms and two public power groups and has an advisory panel of consumer groups, including the American Association of Retired Persons.
"Consumers don't need artificial deadlines," Binz said at a news conference.

The main factor that would affect how much small customers benefit from open markets would be states' policies on whether to let utilities recover in their rates all their investment costs left uncovered by departing customers.
If all stranded costs were put on remaining utility customers, small consumers would gain little benefit from a competitive power market.
Imposing an exit fee on customers that stop buying power from the local utility would ease the burden on remaining customers.

Bills in Congress to require states to deregulate power markets have proposed three different deadlines for action -- the end of 2000, the end of 2003, and January 1999, and proposed guidelines for stranded cost recovery.
The January 1999 deadline was proposed in legislation unveiled Tuesday by third ranking House Republican Rep. Tom DeLay of Texas.
Clinton administration officials and Senate Energy Committee chairman Frank Murkowski have said they would prefer to let states set their own pace.
The Competition Policy Institute's report said the impact of opening power markets would vary a lot from region to region, depending on how expensive electricity was now.

"There are some states whose rates will almost certainly go up with restructuring," said Binz, pointing to states like Oregon and Idaho, which have cheap rates, where utilities would like to be able to sell into higher cost areas.

The institute slammed a report by the conservative Citizens for a Sound Economy (CSE), touted by lawmakers pressing for deregulation, which said in the long run consumers could see a 43 percent cut in their electric bills.
